title: Gas transfer velocity (k600$$ {k}_{600} $$) increases with discharge in steep streams but not in low‐slope streams
content:
Abstract

Gas transfer velocity (k600$$ {\mathrm{k}}_{600} $$) controls gas fluxes between aquatic ecosystems and the atmosphere. In streams, k600$$ {\mathrm{k}}_{600} $$ is controlled by turbulence and, thus, local hydrology and geomorphology. Resultantly, variability in k600$$ {\mathrm{k}}_{600} $$ can be large and modeling k600$$ {\mathrm{k}}_{600} $$ from physical parameters can have large uncertainty. Here, we leverage a large dataset of k600$$ {\mathrm{k}}_{600} $$ estimates derived from tracer-gas experiments in 22 US streams across a range of discharges. Our analysis shows that k600$$ {\mathrm{k}}_{600} $$ was highly variable both spatially across and temporally within streams, with estimates of k600$$ {\mathrm{k}}_{600} $$ spanning three orders of magnitude. Overall, k600$$ {\mathrm{k}}_{600} $$ scaled with discharge in steep streams due to relatively high stream power, but not in low-slope streams, where stream power was relatively low even at high flows. Understanding how k600$$ {\mathrm{k}}_{600} $$ responds to stream discharge in a wide variety of streams is key to creating temporally and spatially resolved estimates of biogeochemical processes in streams.
